title: 2 Samuel 1:17–27
context: David now laments over Saul and over Jonathan his son. He commands that the children of Judah be taught “the song of the bow”, and the narrator notes that it is written in the book of Jashar. The song itself follows: Israel’s glory slain on the high places, a call not to tell it in Gath or Ashkelon, a curse of drought on the mountains of Gilboa, praise of Jonathan’s bow and Saul’s sword, the pairing of father and son in life and in death, a call for the daughters of Israel to weep over Saul, and David’s personal distress over Jonathan, whose love was wonderful, surpassing the love of women. The refrain “How the mighty have fallen!” frames the poem. Both traditions read the unit as a true lament, not as a political performance only, and as the public counterpart of the mourning already begun in verses 11–12. The book of Jashar is a work cited here as the place where this song is written; it is not extant, and its exact character is not agreed. WEB’s wording, “the song of the bow”, treats the piece as a song so named; some read the Hebrew as a command to teach Judah the bow, meaning archery. Those are interpretive options, not a consensus, and not a contrast between the two traditions.

verses.text: David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son
verses.arminianNotes:
David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son. The verse is a heading, and the sentence continues into the parenthesis of verse 18.

Arminian readers hear a real lament, named as such, over both men. David’s grief takes formal, remembered speech, not only the torn clothes and the fast already described.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the introduction to a composed lament over Saul and over Jonathan. The song that follows is David’s, and it is for both the fallen king and the fallen friend.

Both traditions read the heading as shared ground: this is lamentation, and it is over Saul as well as Jonathan.

verses.text: (and he commanded them to teach the children of Judah the song of the bow; behold, it is written in the book of Jashar):
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator adds that David “commanded them to teach the children of Judah the song of the bow; behold, it is written in the book of Jashar”. The lament is to be taught, and a source is named.

Arminian readers hear a public charge to Judah to learn this song. WEB’s phrase “the song of the bow” takes the words as a title or designation of the lament, perhaps echoed later by Jonathan’s bow in verse 22. Some read the Hebrew instead as a command to teach Judah the bow, that is, archery. That question should be left open, not settled as a consensus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same two notices: the command to teach Judah, and the citation of the book of Jashar. That book is also mentioned elsewhere in Scripture; it is not extant, and its exact character is not agreed. No description of it is invented beyond that.

Both traditions take the verse as a heading and a source citation, and they treat the “song of the bow” wording as a known interpretive issue, not as a fork between them.

verses.text: “Your glory, Israel, was slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen!
verses.arminianNotes:
The song begins: “Your glory, Israel, was slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen!” Israel’s glory is named as slain, and the refrain that will return in verses 25 and 27 is already heard.

Arminian readers hear a national loss, not only a private one. The high places of the land have become the scene of the mighty falling, and Israel is addressed as the one whose glory has been slain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take “Your glory, Israel” and “How the mighty have fallen!” as the poem’s opening cry. The lament is for Israel’s sake as well as for the two men; the refrain will structure what follows.

Both traditions read the verse as the start of the song proper, shared ground of public grief.

verses.text: Don’t tell it in Gath. Don’t publish it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t tell it in Gath. Don’t publish it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph.” The news is not to be a song in Philistine streets.

Arminian readers hear a jealous love for Israel’s honor even in defeat. Gath and Ashkelon must not be given this joy; the daughters of the uncircumcised must not triumph in Saul’s and Jonathan’s fall.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same restraint: the lament will be taught in Judah, and it will not be news for the Philistine towns. The fear is that the uncircumcised will rejoice, and the verse refuses them that satisfaction as far as David’s word can refuse it.

Both traditions take the verse as a plea against enemy triumph, shared ground in the poem.

verses.text: You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain on you, and no fields of offerings; for there the shield of the mighty was defiled and cast away, the shield of Saul was not anointed with oil.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain on you, and no fields of offerings; for there the shield of the mighty was defiled and cast away, the shield of Saul was not anointed with oil.” The battlefield itself is placed under a kind of drought-wish.

Arminian readers hear the land of the death being called to share the grief. Gilboa is not to be watered; the shield of Saul, there defiled and cast away, was “not anointed with oil”, a line that may speak of a neglected, unprepared shield, and that some have also heard as an echo of Saul’s own anointing. The second sense should not be pressed as a consensus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the curse of dew and rain, and the defiled shield, as the poem’s way of marking Gilboa. Shields were oiled; “not anointed with oil” can be read in that ordinary sense, and some hear a further overtone. Either way, the verse is about a mighty shield thrown down, not a point of party contrast.

Both traditions read the address to the mountains as part of the lament’s grief over the place of the fall.

verses.text: From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s bow didn’t turn back. Saul’s sword didn’t return empty.
verses.arminianNotes:
“From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s bow didn’t turn back. Saul’s sword didn’t return empty.” Father and son are praised as warriors whose weapons did their work.

Arminian readers hear honor given to both. Jonathan’s bow and Saul’s sword are not spoken of as failures; in the poem they did not turn back or return empty, even though the men have fallen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the pairing of bow and sword, Jonathan and Saul, in the same lines. The song will not divide them in prowess any more than verse 23 will divide them in death. If “the song of the bow” in verse 18 is a title, this verse supplies one reason the name might have been used; that remains only a possible link.

Both traditions take the verse as praise of their warfare, shared ground in the lament.

verses.text: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives. In their death, they were not divided. They were swifter than eagles. They were stronger than lions.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives. In their death, they were not divided. They were swifter than eagles. They were stronger than lions.” The two are held together in life and in death, and then in two images of speed and strength.

Arminian readers hear a refusal to sunder father and son in the telling of their end. Whatever had stood between Saul and David, the lament calls Saul and Jonathan lovely and pleasant, and undivided in death.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the four lines as a unit of praise: lovely and pleasant, not divided in death, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. The poem honors the pair as the poem honors them, not as a later verdict on every act of Saul’s reign.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground of honor for the fallen king and his son together.

verses.text: You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you delicately in scarlet, who put ornaments of gold on your clothing.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you delicately in scarlet, who put ornaments of gold on your clothing.” The daughters of Israel are called to weep, and Saul is remembered as one who clothed them richly.

Arminian readers hear a public, female mourning to match the warning about Philistine daughters in verse 20. Saul is lamented for a generosity in scarlet and gold, a human good the song will not withhold from him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same summons to weep, and the same memory of scarlet and gold. The lament finds something in Saul’s reign to mourn as a loss for the daughters of Israel, not only a theological verdict.

Both traditions take the verse as a call to weep over Saul, shared ground in the middle of the poem.

verses.text: How the mighty have fallen in the middle of the battle! Jonathan was slain on your high places.
verses.arminianNotes:
“How the mighty have fallen in the middle of the battle! Jonathan was slain on your high places.” The refrain returns, and then the song turns, more narrowly, to Jonathan.

Arminian readers hear the general cry focused now on Jonathan, slain on the high places already named in verse 19. The next verse will make David’s grief for him still more personal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the refrain and the naming of Jonathan as the turn toward the friend. He is slain “on your high places”, Israel’s heights, in the middle of the battle.

Both traditions read the verse as the bridge from the public lament to David’s address to Jonathan, on shared ground.

verses.text: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan. You have been very pleasant to me. Your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan. You have been very pleasant to me. Your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.” David speaks to Jonathan as brother, and he names a love that was wonderful and incomparable in the terms the poem uses.

Arminian readers hear a genuine, personal distress. The language of brother and of wonderful love belongs to a covenant friendship of extraordinary depth; the verse is not a place to force a later debate as if it were the poem’s own subject, or to treat any one modern reading as consensus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the distress, the address “my brother Jonathan”, and the wonderful love as the climax of David’s grief for him. The comparison “surpassing the love of women” is the song’s own measure of that bond; it should be read as the lament states it, without being turned into a contrast between the two traditions.

Both traditions receive the verse as David’s personal mourning for Jonathan, shared ground of affection and loss.

verses.text: How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!”
verses.arminianNotes:
The song closes, “How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!” The refrain returns a last time, and the weapons themselves are said to have perished.

Arminian readers hear an ending that gathers the whole: the mighty have fallen, and the very tools of their war are gone. The lament does not end in a call to seize the throne, but in that fall.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same close. The weapons of war have perished with the mighty; the poem ends where it began, in the falling of the strong, and then gives way to the next chapter’s inquiry of the LORD.

Both traditions take the final refrain as the right end of the lament, shared ground, leaving David’s kingship to the word of God that follows.
